tasks.task: ## What Link the engine release from `engine-incremental-read`, make the browser receive only what changed and only for what is on screen, and hold it to the five budgets below. `dag-ui-project-centric-spike-request-load-report` is the design source: its pushed-changes prototype is the design (cursor reads were measured and rejected, because they still re-read one sidebar row per change anywhere on the host), its harness under `apps/dag-ui-e2e/spikes/` is what this task grows into telemetry, and its baseline is the "before". Its 13 numbered findings are the list of pollers and re-reads to remove. 1. **Pushed changes on the event stream.** The read API's event stream carries the changes themselves for what the page subscribes to: a trimmed sidebar row per changed run, carrying only the fields the sidebar renders (stated in `docs/contract.md`; no whole row, no field the sidebar does not show); a patch of the open run's detail; a patch of the visible timeline (Overall or one node's); and the Channel queue's changes. The page subscribes only to its visible view: switching among Graph, Overall, a node's timeline and Channel changes the subscription, and a hidden view is neither read nor subscribed. No frame repeats a full snapshot of state the page already holds: a connection opens with no run-list snapshot restating the list the page just read (the run-scoped stream sends none at all), and a reconnect resumes from the last frame received. A change is never answered with a full payload in place of a patch. 2. **Incremental server side.** The server keeps each subscribed run's `RunView` current with `RunView::refresh` and builds detail and timeline patches from the records `Appended { first }` names, rebuilding a payload whole only on `Reread`. 3. **Removed polls and re-reads.** The 10 s status poll (`STATUS_POLL_MS`), the per-change re-reads of the run row, the projects list, the run status, `/api/v2/unwatched` and the Channel queue, and the full detail and timeline refetches all go. `/api/v2/unwatched` is read only by the Host page, when it opens and on its refresh control. A settled or stopped run's page, once loaded, sends no request beyond what the page with nothing open sends. 4. **Contract.** `docs/contract.md` states the subscription parameters, every frame type and its fields, the resume behaviour and the removed snapshot, with the versions moved by its convention, mirrored in `packages/dag-model`'s schema. 5. **Telemetry.** A load journey grown from the spike's harness, in its own Playwright config run by a new `dag-ui-e2e:test-load` target (so `dag-ui-e2e:test` keeps its length), drives every page state over the corpus the workload below states, one variant per invocation on a freshly generated corpus (the report's harness caveat), and records into `apps/dag-ui-e2e/telemetry/request-load.json`: requests per minute by route, frames and bytes by type and stream, repeated snapshot frames and bytes, and each appended record's lag. Lag is measured per record, append to display, on every view: the writer stamps each record's append; on the node timeline, whose rows carry each record's journal sequence number as a data attribute, the lag runs to that row's appearance in the DOM; on Graph, Overall and Channel, each view's root carries the journal sequence number of the last record whose change it has rendered (set after the view's DOM update for that change is committed, as a `data-journal-seq` attribute), and the lag of each record runs to the moment a DOM observer sees that attribute reach its sequence number. Frame arrival is recorded in the breakdown, never as the figure. 6. **Budgets.** Register the five budgets below in a new `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml` with a `dag-ui-e2e:budgets` target running `onebudgetspec check` over it, as `github-workflows:budgets` does over `.github/budgets.yaml`, cached on the telemetry file. Each command is the one generic runner `apps/dag-ui-e2e/request-load-budget.mjs`, which reads the telemetry, reports the figure and its breakdown in `detail` through the onebudgetspec reporter, and compares nothing itself. **Server CPU telemetry.** Extend the same `dag-ui-e2e:test-load` target and `apps/dag-ui-e2e/telemetry/request-load.json` to record server-process-tree CPU time during the live observation windows. Run one-tab and two-tab variants of Graph, Overall, node timeline and Channel, with both tabs on the same state. Start every measured state/tab-count variant with a fresh server and freshly generated corpus: do not reuse a growing server across variants or subtract an estimated drift. Divide total server CPU seconds by the 120-second window and tab count, including idle server work; exclude browser and corpus-writer processes. The generic runner’s `--metric cpu` reads this recorded telemetry only, reports the maximum per-tab cores and page/tab-count/total-CPU breakdown, and compares nothing. Register this budget beside the other four in `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml`, labelled `host`; keep its measurement in the dedicated load target and out of ordinary e2e. No new dedicated fixture or wrapper is needed. Raise any target miss to the manager without loosening it. ## Why The Observatory stays open for hours beside many runs on a host several managers share. Today it re-reads whole payloads on every change anywhere on the host (about 800 requests and 14 to 19 MB a minute on a run that finished long ago, and up to 226 MB a minute on a live run's Overall view), polls on a timer, and one tab on a live run keeps the server up to four cores busy. Receiving only changes, and only for what is on screen, makes the view quiet on the server, cheap on the host and quick to show a new record, and the budgets keep later work from bringing the noise back. ## Budgets ### Browser requests per minute on a finished run's page - **Id:** `dag-ui-settled-requests-per-minute` - **Measure:** HTTP requests the Observatory's browser sends per minute with a settled or stopped run open while other runs on the host change, the most expensive of that run's Graph, Overall and node timeline views; detail reports each view's figure, the figure with nothing open under the same activity, and the requests by route. - **Target:** at most 1 requests/min - **Basis:** measured - **Measurement source:** telemetry - **Check runtime:** approximately 2 seconds - **Workload:** The e2e corpus at this host's scale: 150 run directories across 30 projects (1 open run, 10 other live runs, 10 stopped, 129 settled); the 10 other live runs each appended 50 journal records per minute (the p90 active-minute rate of 54 recorded runs on this host, median 8) with one 400-record burst in the window; one browser tab; each view held 120 s after load. The open run is settled or stopped and its journal does not change. - **Evidence:** dag-ui-project-centric-spike-request-load-report, at this workload: today 759 to 800.5 requests/min (per-change row, projects, status and unwatched re-reads, against 601.5 with nothing open); the pushed-changes prototype 0.5 (one unwatched read as the window opened, which this plan removes from run pages) against 0 with nothing open. - **Command:** `node apps/dag-ui-e2e/request-load-budget.mjs --telemetry apps/dag-ui-e2e/telemetry/request-load.json --metric settled` - **Registered in:** `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml` of `github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline-ui`, an entry this task adds ### Browser requests per minute on a live run - **Id:** `dag-ui-live-requests-per-minute` - **Measure:** HTTP requests the Observatory's browser sends per minute with a live run open while its journal and other runs' journals grow, the most expensive of its Graph, Overall, node timeline and Channel views; detail reports each view's figure and its requests by route. - **Target:** at most 2 requests/min - **Basis:** measured - **Measurement source:** telemetry - **Check runtime:** approximately 2 seconds - **Workload:** The e2e corpus at this host's scale: 150 run directories across 30 projects (1 open run, 10 other live runs, 10 stopped, 129 settled); the 10 other live runs each appended 50 journal records per minute (the p90 active-minute rate of 54 recorded runs on this host, median 8) with one 400-record burst in the window; one browser tab; each view held 120 s after load. The open run is live, its journal grown to 116,000 records (this host's largest) and appended 50 records per minute, taking the burst. - **Evidence:** dag-ui-project-centric-spike-request-load-report, at this workload: today Graph 238.5, Overall 220, node timeline 236.5 and Channel 384.5 requests/min; the pushed-changes prototype 0, 0, 0 and 11, the 11 being Channel's queue read, which the prototype left unpushed and this task pushes. - **Command:** `node apps/dag-ui-e2e/request-load-budget.mjs --telemetry apps/dag-ui-e2e/telemetry/request-load.json --metric live` - **Registered in:** `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml` of `github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline-ui`, an entry this task adds ### Seconds before a new record shows on a live run's page - **Id:** `dag-ui-live-update-lag-seconds` - **Measure:** The 95th-percentile time from a record being appended to the open live run's journal until the page has rendered it (the node timeline's row for that record appearing, or Graph, Overall or Channel marking that record's change rendered), per record, over every record appended in the window, the slowest of the four views; detail reports each view's p50, p95 and maximum, the p95 during the burst, and the frame-arrival time as a breakdown. - **Target:** at most 3 seconds - **Basis:** design - **Measurement source:** telemetry - **Check runtime:** approximately 2 seconds - **Workload:** The e2e corpus at this host's scale: 150 run directories across 30 projects (1 open run, 10 other live runs, 10 stopped, 129 settled); the 10 other live runs each appended 50 journal records per minute (the p90 active-minute rate of 54 recorded runs on this host, median 8) with one 400-record burst in the window; one browser tab; each view held 120 s after load. The open run is live, its journal grown to 116,000 records (this host's largest) and appended 50 records per minute, taking the burst. - **Evidence:** dag-ui-project-centric-spike-request-load-report, at this workload, read off the turn count and the live-activity line rather than per record (so approximate): worst-view p95 10.84 s today, 12.28 s for the pushed-changes prototype and 10.96 s for cursor reads, each floored by a full re-read and fold of the 116,000-record journal per change (3 to 31 s per read). engine-incremental-read removes that floor; what remains by design is the server's 500 ms journal check, one fold of the appended records and one pushed frame, so 3 s holds with headroom for the burst. - **Command:** `node apps/dag-ui-e2e/request-load-budget.mjs --telemetry apps/dag-ui-e2e/telemetry/request-load.json --metric lag` - **Registered in:** `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml` of `github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline-ui`, an entry this task adds ### Megabytes per minute the browser receives - **Id:** `dag-ui-wire-megabytes-per-minute` - **Measure:** Megabytes the Observatory's browser receives per minute (encoded bytes of every response and event-stream frame), the most expensive page state; detail reports each page state's figure, its bytes by frame type and route, and the repeated full-snapshot frames and bytes, including load and a reconnect. - **Target:** at most 0.3 MB/min - **Basis:** estimate - **Measurement source:** telemetry - **Check runtime:** approximately 2 seconds - **Workload:** The e2e corpus at this host's scale: 150 run directories across 30 projects (1 open run, 10 other live runs, 10 stopped, 129 settled); the 10 other live runs each appended 50 journal records per minute (the p90 active-minute rate of 54 recorded runs on this host, median 8) with one 400-record burst in the window; one browser tab; each view held 120 s after load. Taken over every page state: nothing open, a settled run and a stopped run on Graph, Overall and a node timeline, the live run as above on Graph, Overall, a node timeline and Channel, and the Host page. - **Evidence:** Estimate from dag-ui-project-centric-spike-request-load-report, at this workload: today 13.8 to 19.0 MB/min with nothing open or a finished run open and up to 225.7 MB/min on the live run's Overall view; the pushed-changes prototype 0.21 to 0.68 MB/min, of which 0.4 to 0.5 MB/min was about 495 whole sidebar rows per minute at about 990 bytes each. Trimming each pushed row to the fields the sidebar renders (estimated at no more than 200 bytes) leaves about 0.1 MB/min of rows, plus the measured patches (timeline 41 to 83 KB/min, detail 3 to 5 KB/min), so about 0.2 MB/min in the worst state; 0.3 leaves headroom. This task's telemetry measures it. - **Command:** `node apps/dag-ui-e2e/request-load-budget.mjs --telemetry apps/dag-ui-e2e/telemetry/request-load.json --metric wire` - **Registered in:** `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml` of `github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline-ui`, an entry this task adds ### Server CPU cores per live browser tab - **Id:** `dag-ui-server-cpu-cores-per-live-tab` - **Measure:** Maximum server-process-tree CPU seconds divided by 120 observation seconds and by live tab count, across one-tab and two-tab variants of Graph, Overall, node timeline and Channel. Includes the server’s total CPU without idle-baseline subtraction; excludes browser and fixture-writer processes. Detail reports total CPU seconds, average total cores, per-tab cores, tab count and page state. - **Target:** at most 0.5 cores/live-tab - **Basis:** estimate - **Measurement source:** telemetry - **Check runtime:** approximately 2 seconds - **Workload:** 150 run directories across 30 projects, 10 other live runs each appending 50 records/minute and one 400-record burst; the open live run has 116,000 journal records and appends 50 records/minute taking the burst. One-tab and two-tab variants each open the same live page state (Graph, Overall, node timeline or Channel), each held 120 seconds after load. Each variant starts from a fresh generated corpus and fresh server, avoiding cross-state CPU drift. - **Evidence:** Manager-approved estimate, not a measured post-change CPU figure: dag-ui-project-centric-spike-request-load-report measured 1.3–4.1 cores per live tab with whole-journal reads and folds. Reading, parsing and folding only appended records is the design basis for the estimated 0.5-core target. The manager approved the threshold and 1-/2-tab measurement and required eliminating state-order drift; fresh server per variant is chosen. Generic telemetry-only JSON analysis is estimated at 2 seconds, matching the existing runner’s small-file analysis; no scenario is executed by the budget command. - **Command:** `node apps/dag-ui-e2e/request-load-budget.mjs --telemetry apps/dag-ui-e2e/telemetry/request-load.json --metric cpu` - **Registered in:** `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml` of `github.com/nickderobertis/onepipeline-ui`, an entry this task adds ## Acceptance criteria - The budgets `dag-ui-settled-requests-per-minute` (a settled or stopped run open) and `dag-ui-live-requests-per-minute` (the live run open, its journal at 116,000 records growing 50 records per minute) are registered in `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml`, each command reporting its figure from the telemetry `dag-ui-e2e:test-load` recorded at the workload of 150 run directories across 30 projects with 10 other live runs each growing 50 records per minute and one 400-record burst, each view held 120 s. - The budget `dag-ui-live-update-lag-seconds` is registered in the same file and its command reports the per-record 95th-percentile append-to-display lag from that telemetry at the live workload above, measured per record as the task states rather than off a turn count. - The budget `dag-ui-wire-megabytes-per-minute` is registered in the same file and its command reports the megabytes received per minute in the most expensive page state from that telemetry, over every page state at that workload, with the repeated snapshot frames and bytes in its breakdown. - `dag-ui-e2e:budgets` passes on the finished tree over telemetry the finished tree's `dag-ui-e2e:test-load` recorded. - A Playwright journey over the real server, while other runs' journals are being appended to, records the requests of the page with nothing open and then of a settled run and of a stopped run open on each of Graph, Overall and a node timeline, and asserts that the run pages send no request the page with nothing open did not send. - A Playwright journey over the real server shows that a record appended to the open live run appears on its Graph, Overall and node timeline views with no request for the run's detail or timeline and no full-payload frame, that a change on another run arrives as one sidebar row frame whose keys are exactly the sidebar fields `docs/contract.md` lists, and that a surface raised on the live run appears on its Channel tab with no request for the Channel queue. - A Playwright journey asserts that the page receives no run-list snapshot frame after its first list read, on first connection and after the test forces the event stream to reconnect, and that switching the live run among Graph, Channel and a node timeline changes the subscription so the view it left is no longer subscribed or read. - The final report compares requests per minute and megabytes per minute for every page state before (the spike evidence) and after (finished-tree telemetry), and append-to-display lag where an append changes that view. Unavailable baseline figures and inapplicable lag on unchanged settled/stopped views are explicitly identified, without invented comparisons. The report also gives finished-tree server CPU totals and per-tab results by live page state and tab count against the spike’s 1.3–4.1-core evidence, identifying differing or unavailable baseline variants rather than claiming a matched measurement. - The tests over the code this change touches are green on the finished tree: `dag-ui:test`, `dag-model:test`, `telemetry-client:test`, `dag-ui-e2e:test`, `dag-ui-e2e:test-load` and the crate's tests. - The judged llmlint tier of `onepipeline-ui` over this change's diff against its base reports no failing rule. - A real-server Playwright journey disconnects the event stream, appends identifiable changes while disconnected, reconnects from the last received frame and observes every change exactly once in the rendered views without repeated snapshot. Switching among Graph, Overall, Channel and node timeline leaves every hidden view unsubscribed and unread. - Real-server functional tests use real journal appends and RunView::refresh, with passive parse/fold and payload-construction instrumentation rather than replacing those layers: Appended parses and folds only suffix records and builds detail/timeline patches from them; full rebuild occurs only on Reread after initial load. The served stream frames validate against dag-model and match docs/contract.md’s fields, resume rules and version convention. - Every claim the dispatch makes about the finished implementation, verification and evidence remains accurate for the final tree. Evidence from an earlier tree is explicitly identified as such, with subsequent changes and corrections stated; no superseded result is presented as verification of the finished tree. - A real-server test changes the run label overlay without journal growth and proves refresh returns Reread and the rebuilt served view matches fresh open; the consumer follows the corrected Unchanged/Appended/Reread contract. - `dag-ui-server-cpu-cores-per-live-tab` is registered in `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml` at the manager-approved estimated maximum 0.5 cores/live-tab, labelled host. Its generic command reports the maximum total server-process-tree CPU seconds / 120 seconds / tab count from recorded `dag-ui-e2e:test-load` telemetry for Graph, Overall, node timeline and Channel, with 1 and 2 tabs on each state, over 150 runs / 30 projects, 10 other live runs at 50 records/minute and one 400-record burst, the open live journal at 116,000 records appending 50 records/minute. Every variant uses a fresh server and corpus; detail includes totals and per-page/tab-count breakdown. The existing `dag-ui-e2e:budgets` pass covers this budget too; tests record figures without asserting nonfunctional thresholds. ## Spike evidence This task builds on these spikes. Start from each report's measurements and from the harness on each branch rather than measuring again. A report is the document of this plan's own project with that id or, on a copy of the plan, the one whose `onetaskgraph.origin` names it: - `spike-request-load`: report `dag-ui-project-centric-spike-request-load-report`, a document of this plan's own project; branch `nick/dag-ui-project-centric/spike-request-load` ## Additional info **The contracts this task states are shared with other nodes of the plan and are fixed for the run.** If you find a departure you want (a missing field, a wrong shape, a better split), raise it with the manager through `$ORCHESTRATOR_ASK_MANAGER` as a proposal and keep building against the agreed surface; never change a shared surface on your own. **Budget measurement, decided.** All four figures are read from telemetry, never measured fresh by a budget command: the load journeys of `dag-ui-e2e:test-load`, in the `dag-ui-e2e` project, record them into `apps/dag-ui-e2e/telemetry/request-load.json`, and that project registers all four in its own `apps/dag-ui-e2e/budgets.yaml`. No budget carries a label. The journeys assert behaviour (which requests, frames and subscriptions occur and which do not), never a count, size or lag against a threshold; thresholds live only in the budgets file. The `test-load` target runs on Linux only and adds no macOS job, so the repository's `.github/budgets.yaml` macOS budgets are untouched. **An estimated threshold is still the requirement.** `dag-ui-wire-megabytes-per-minute`'s 0.3 MB/min is an estimate until this task's telemetry measures it, and `dag-ui-live-update-lag-seconds`'s 3 s rests on design. If the finished page measures above either, raise it with the manager through `$ORCHESTRATOR_ASK_MANAGER` with the figure and its breakdown; never loosen a threshold in the budgets file on your own. This node waits for the published `crate` release of `engine-incremental-read`; the version arrives in a note when it does. The spike's harness and prototype are on its preserved branch, named under Spike evidence; carry what serves the budgets into this repository's own tree rather than its `spikes/` directory. ## Additional info ### Operational notes for this host **Run only the checks that exercise what you changed.** The tests that cover the code you touched, the lint that reads your diff — and nothing wider. The repository's own automation runs the full bar downstream on the change this work becomes: a `pre-push` hook where that repository publishes locally, the host's required checks where it publishes remotely. Neither is waiting for you to have run it first, so running it here spends twenty to forty minutes of this dispatch learning what the merge path reports anyway. That is measured rather than estimated: one node in this workstream spent about 84 minutes on three rounds of everything its repository could run, to reach lint findings a diff-scoped run reports in two. **Pick those checks from your change, and take the narrowest scope each one supports.** One test module over the whole suite; the lint over your diff over the lint over the tree. A repository's own fast deterministic tier is a fine choice when it is what exercises your change — its `just --list` says which recipe that is — and a poor one when you reached for it because it was the widest thing available. When a check you ran reports something, fix that and run **that check** again; nothing here asks you to re-run its neighbours to confirm, and a wider tier cannot re-check a finding it never made. **A dispatch that changed nothing tracked owes none of them.** When your deliverable is a document, a report, or an answer, there is no changed code for those checks to exercise and you are complete without them — decide that from what the repository shows, never because running them is slow or inconvenient. `git status` reporting nothing to commit is then a correct and complete outcome, not a problem to solve by writing a file nobody asked for. **A publication check runs downstream, so no worker can run it and none is judged on it.** The host's required checks and a repository's `pre-push` gate run on the change this work becomes, after this dispatch settles: downstream publication checks are not runnable by a worker, and a dispatch is never held to one having passed. That holds on a retry too. A `checks-failed` retry — a re-dispatch onto the same branch carrying the merge path's refusal and `onevcs`'s evidence — is judged on its task's stated local acceptance checks: the repair of what the refusal named, proven by the checks the task names, and never by the downstream check passing again, which can only happen once the retry has settled. One retry that fixed and locally verified the failing test its refusal named was failed for not re-running the required check, which left finished work unpublished and its dependents skipped until a manager published it by hand. **Never signal a process you did not identify by PID, and a PID you got from a pattern is still a pattern kill.** Several managers share this host, and their dispatches, drivers, publications and test servers run under the same few binary names — `just`, `node`, `python`, `onepipeline-api` — so a kill by name knows nothing about *whose* work it matched. The distinction is the tool rather than the pattern: `pgrep` and `ps` **read**, and either spelling of them is fine, `pgrep -x` included; `pkill` **signals**, and it is never the answer here, in any spelling. `-x` is the trap, because it reads as the careful one — `pkill -f 'just gate'` at least needs a narrowing pattern, while `pkill -x just` takes every `just` on the machine. Reading the table first and piping the pids into `kill` is no way around it: that is the same pattern kill with more steps. Two workers reached that place from different directions on 2026-08-24, while another manager's dispatch had been live over an hour. One ran `pkill -TERM -x just`. The other ran `ps -eo pid,args | grep 'onepipeline-api serve' | awk '{print $1}' | while read pid; do kill "$pid"; done` — which obeys the letter of every paragraph below and does the same damage, because `just dag-ui` and the e2e suites both spawn that server and a pytest run's were alive at that moment. **The one process you may signal is one you started yourself, so capture its PID as you start it:** cmd & MYPID=$! kill "$MYPID" Anything you did not start belongs to somebody. Read what it is, report what you found, and leave it running. **A wait written against a full command line never ends, because one of those command lines is yours.** That is a different defect from the one above — it wedges your own dispatch rather than somebody else's — and it is why `pgrep -f` cannot be waited on. `pgrep -f` matches its pattern against every process's whole argv and excludes exactly one process — itself — never the shell that invoked it. So any pattern naming the thing you are waiting for is, by construction, a substring of the command line of the shell doing the waiting: `until ! pgrep -f "just gate"` matches its own loop and never exits, and so does the same loop written against the judged lint tier's script, `scripts/fetch-corpus.sh`, or `publish-branch`. That is a defect in the polling mechanism rather than a fact about gates, so it applies to every wait you write. That has wedged four workers here, and then two more workers and the manager itself in one night: seven instances of one defect. A crozier corpus audit waited in `until ! pgrep -f 'scripts/fetch-corpus.sh'` with no fetch running at all — the only two matches were its own polling shell and the manager's diagnostic shell — and waited until it was interrupted. A `check-plan-bar-conflict` dispatch waited on `! pgrep -f` naming the judged lint tier's script, whose negation could never become true, and was cancelled and killed; its replacement then reached for `pkill -f` against three patterns, which is not a wait at all but the same self-match with a signal attached, and is refused above. And the manager, an hour after instructing a worker about this, guarded a launch with `pgrep -f "publish-branch" && echo ABORT || launch`, whose pattern was a literal substring of the launching shell's own command line: it aborted unconditionally and then reported a publish as RUNNING that did not exist. That last one is the evidence that matters most — a rule its own author reproduces an hour after issuing it is a rule whose wording is the problem rather than its reader. **Wait with a sentinel file.** Background the whole command you are waiting on — one command, so that what you waited on is what you meant to run — and poll for a file only that invocation can write: ( just test > /tmp/check.$$.log 2>&1; echo $? > /tmp/check.$$.exit ) & until [ -f /tmp/check.$$.exit ]; do sleep 20; done **A process must finish inside the turn that started it.** Backgrounding is how you wait on a slow command *within* one turn, which is why the launch and the wait sit together in that example — both halves belong to the same turn. What does not survive is a background process left running when the turn ends: nothing carries it across, and the launch gives you no sign of that, because it succeeded and the turn then ended normally. The loss shows up a turn later as a sentinel that never appeared and a recipe terminated by signal, with the whole run to pay for again. It bites hardest where it is most tempting, because a worker reaches for backgrounding exactly when a command is slow enough to threaten the turn — here the judged lint tier and a whole test tier, which are the two runs a node most needs to have made. So run a slow check in the foreground, or background it and wait out its sentinel before your turn ends; never end a turn intending to read a result on the next one. **To ask whether a process is running at all, match the executable, not the command line.** `pgrep -x onepipeline` matches process *names* exactly — the binary, not its arguments — so the shell doing the asking, whose own name is `bash`, cannot match it however the pattern is spelled. Where the binary name is not distinctive enough to identify what you mean (`just`, `node` and `python` run everything), read the process table instead and drop the one self-match that form has: ps -eo pid,args | grep -v grep | grep 'lint-llm-diff' Both of those are **reads**, which is what makes `-x` safe here and forbidden the moment the tool signals. The replacement for the worker wedged above reached for `pkill -f "just gate"`, `pkill -f "just check"` and `pkill -f "nx run"` while another manager's run was live. Read to learn what is running, report what you found, and signal nothing you did not start. **One sentinel and one log per invocation, and look before you launch one.** That pair is a shape rather than two literal paths. Several dispatches run on this host at once and they share `/tmp`, so a second worker writing `/tmp/check.log` writes into the first one's — and `until [ -f /tmp/check.exit ]` returns immediately on somebody else's exit file, reporting their result as yours. Name both after the invocation (`/tmp/check.$$.log`, or the node id), and, before starting it, check whether its sentinel path is already in use by another invocation; if so, choose a different invocation-specific pair. This path-ownership check does not prohibit concurrent checks or judged tiers. Three workers collided on shared names today and not one of the three failures read as what it was: two deterministic-tier runs deadlocked against the same cargo target-directory lock, so both logs sat unchanged and neither progressed — about fifteen minutes lost and three interruptions to a live turn; two whole-e2e runs wrote to one log, and stopping the duplicate left four `SIGTERM` entries in it that read exactly like real test failures; two judged-tier runs raced and wasted a roll, which was harmless only by luck. Read a log that has stopped growing as two commands blocking each other before you read it as one command working. **Write the files this dispatch needs under `ONEPIPELINE_NODE_SCRATCH_DIR`, rather than under a `/tmp` path you invented.** It is an absolute path to a directory that exists and is writable when the dispatch starts, is unique to this dispatch, and is not removed while it runs. **Root-owned files after a container run.** The pre-push visual guard captures in Docker as root and can leave `.nx/` and `dist/` unwritable, failing the *next* check with `NX Permission denied (os error 13)`. There is no passwordless sudo; repair from inside a container: docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.61.1-noble \ chown -R "$(id -u):$(id -g)" /w **If a test fails in a way that makes no sense, check the host before the test.** On 2026-08-19 two publication attempts against the same already-green branch failed on two unrelated tests — a 5-second timeout, then a browser remote that never came up — and both were written up as flakes. The host was at 197G/197G, and the next attempt said so outright with `No space left on device`. A full disk does not announce itself to a test runner; it announces itself as an unrelated test failing. One command rules it out: df -h /home . **If a rule looks wrong or misapplied, say so with evidence rather than editing it.** **One suppression policy, and this is the whole of it.** A site-scoped `ignore` directive is permitted where the rule is genuinely misapplied at that site **and** the directive carries a substantive reason saying why. What is forbidden is silencing a finding you have not answered so that a count moves. What you owe an account of is **every suppression your own diff writes — added, moved or rewritten — and every one already standing over a line that diff changes** — each with its site and its reason, in your completion report, so the manager reads what you left rather than discovering it. Both halves are decided from the diff alone: a directive line inside it, or a changed line inside the region a directive covers. A file-scoped directive is outside both unless your diff writes the directive itself — its region is every line of the file, so counting it would make this file's own header a debt of every change that edits a word of it. Suppressions elsewhere in the tree are not yours to inventory: this repository carries several hundred standing directives, and a list of them would be longer than the report is read under while saying nothing about the change under review. That scope is stated because the sentence it replaces read two ways at once: its first clause reached every directive anywhere in the repository, while its second — *so the manager reads what you left* — was about this dispatch's own work, in the same breath. A node was failed on the wider reading for not accounting for suppressions it had never touched, on a tree whose every target had just run from cold and come back green; it cost a third dispatch of a run's final node. The reading above is the one the purpose clause and the scale both support, and it is written so that a worker complying with it and a judge reading it adversarially land in the same place. It says which lines rather than which sites for the same reason: *site* was itself readable two ways, and the first worker to apply the sentence could not decide whether the file-scoped directives at the head of `AGENTS.md` were owed by a change that edits one of its paragraphs. Apply that same test to whatever replaces it: read it as a worker trying to comply and as a judge looking for a way to refuse, and if the two can land in different places it is not one source yet. `AGENTS.md` states no suppression policy of its own and points here, because this file is what your judge reads beside your task: while that document said it twice, one dispatch added four site-scoped ignores each carrying a substantive reason and was failed for *"the task's categorical instruction never to suppress a rule"* — work that was correct under one of this repository's own readings and refused under the other. **`--no-verify` is not an acceptable response to a slow or inconvenient hook.** The hooks are this repository's enforcement point — there is no CI — so bypassing one commits work that nothing has checked, and nothing you run afterwards catches it: a check runs over the finished tree, by which point a bypassed commit is simply history. Two workers today reached for `git commit --no-verify`, both on a commit they had judged mechanical, and one of the two was a *merge* commit — a conflict resolution, which is the single most likely commit in a dispatch to be wrong. No check caught either one; the monitor caught both. If a hook is slow, wait for it. If it refuses, it is telling you something about the commit in front of you, and the answer is to fix the commit. **Commit a coherent working piece the moment it works.** A dirty worktree does not survive this dispatch: what is uncommitted when your last turn ends is what nothing recovers — not a retry, not a recovery verb, not a manager reading the branch. So each piece is its own commit as you finish it, rather than one commit held back to the end. *The moment it works* is the moment you have seen it work: the checks that piece needs are run before it is committed rather than after, so that each commit is one you have evidence for. **Ask rather than stop.** When you cannot proceed without a decision that is not yours — a frozen contract you would have to amend, a goal that reads two ways, a constraint you would have to relax — put the question to your manager over `$ORCHESTRATOR_ASK_MANAGER`, which every dispatch carries, and go on working on whatever does not depend on the answer. Ending your turns with the work undone and the question unasked is the one response nothing can recover: a worker that reasoned about a frozen contract correctly, declined to amend it unilaterally, named two options for its owner, and then stopped for three turns lost about fifteen minutes of correct work and settled reporting `ahead of main: 0 commit(s)`. **Draft a follow-up that can wait; never draft one that cannot.** Work you notice that is outside your subtask — a bug beside the code you touched, a missing test or script, a stale document, an improvement to this harness or to the context agents are given — is a follow-up, and doing it is not yours. Record each one the moment you notice it by piping its body into `"$ORCHESTRATOR_FOLLOW_UP_DRAFT"`, whose `--help` names the flags and the four headings that body carries; the command stamps where it came from. Do not collect them into a list at the end of your last message instead, because nothing reads that list. A draft is unverified — a follow-up agent checks every one after the run — and it is not your completion report, which still says what you did. Drafting is only for what can wait: anything blocking, whether a decision fork, a constraint you cannot meet, or something your manager should act on now, goes over `$ORCHESTRATOR_ASK_MANAGER` immediately, as the paragraph above says, and is never drafted in its place. **A GitHub rate-limit refusal that `gh api rate_limit` disagrees with is the secondary limiter.** The primary limit is the one that endpoint reports and the one a wait answers. The secondary limiter is reported by nothing, polled by nothing, and not waited out by polling — every further attempt extends it. So when a `gh` call is refused for a rate limit while `gh api rate_limit` still shows budget, stop making that call: deliver the result another way, name in your report what was refused and what you tried, and leave the retry to a person. **Publication goes through the harness.** The session branch reaches its remote only through `onevcs publish "$ONEVCS_SESSION"`, and its change request is lifted, landed or kept for the user's review by the lifecycle after you settle. No `git push` of the session branch, no `gh pr create` for it, no `gh pr ready`, no `gh pr merge`. Finish the branch, commit everything, leave the tree clean, and report. Landing it is explicitly **not** yours to perform and **not** part of your acceptance criteria. Two things are yours, and each only when this task's own `## Additional info` — its own words above these notes — says so: - **Only when the task's `## Additional info` says the change request may be published early**: `onevcs publish "$ONEVCS_SESSION" --draft [--title T] [--body-file PATH]` opens the session's change request as a draft, and a later `publish --draft` pushes new commits onto that same change request and never opens a second. Commit everything first — a dirty tree is committed for you, under a provenance you did not choose. `onevcs change describe "$ONEVCS_SESSION" --body-file PATH` replaces its description and `onevcs change show "$ONEVCS_SESSION"` reads it back. The description you leave is what the drafter finishes from, so start it with what only you know — the evidence and where it is. Never mark the draft ready yourself; after you finish, the lifecycle lifts it or keeps it as a draft for the user's review according to the repository's policy. `ONEVCS_SESSION` is in every lifecycle dispatch's environment. - **Only when the task's `## Additional info` authorizes a throwaway demonstration change request**: after the draft is open, cut a branch from the session branch, commit the demonstration on it, push it with `git push -u origin `, open it with `gh pr create --draft --base --head --title "DO NOT MERGE: …"`, capture the evidence — `gh pr view --comments`, `gh pr checks `, and `gh api` **reads** of that change request's own comments, checks and reviews, never a write to anything — then close it with `gh pr close --delete-branch`, return to the session branch, and delete the local branch — a local branch left behind makes the session's close refuse. Its base is always the session branch, never the repository's base; it is never marked ready; it is closed before you finish. Everything else a push or a change-request verb could do is still not yours. **A branch you resume may already be on its remote, and a published branch only grows.** A retry — a `checks-failed` one among them — re-dispatches onto the same branch, which an earlier publication may already have pushed. So check before you touch its history: `git fetch` and `git log origin/`, or the published commit your task's context names. The repair of a branch already on its remote is new commits on top of the remote's commit — never an amend, a rebase, a squash, a reset or a force-push of commits already there. One retry that fixed both refusals its merge path named by amending the two commits already pushed was refused `non-fast-forward` when it published, and settled `push-rejected` with the correct tree stranded on the host. **Every claim you make about the finished work is true of the tree as it finally stands.** That is the property you are held to, and it says nothing about where your report sits. This conversation does not end when you report — your supervisor keeps asking, and answering well means running things — so a report required to be this dispatch's literal final output is one no correct worker can give. What is required instead is that nothing you have said about the work is untrue of the tree by the time you stop. When work follows your report, say in that same turn what changed and what you re-ran. A correct delta satisfies this exactly as fully as restating the whole report does. Silence does not satisfy it at all. Your last substantive turn should leave a reader able to say what the finished tree contains and what was verified about it, whether that comes from one report or from a report plus the deltas after it. **A claim about a check, a test, a lint run, or a commit that was not run or was not made is false, and fails on its merits.** A report asserting a check passed on a commit where no such run occurred is that case, and one node of this host's history was correctly failed for it. So do not carry a claim forward across a change that could have invalidated it — re-run what the change could have broken, or say which claims you have not re-checked. **Evidence deliberately about an earlier or induced state is not a false claim.** Proving that an assertion can fail means making it fail, reading the message, and reverting; proving that a message used to say nothing means quoting the run from before the change. A citation of a run taken before a change, or of a failure induced on purpose as evidence, is correct evidence — provided the citation says which it is. One node of this host was failed for exactly that: its own criteria required its assertions be observed failing, and the resulting-tree property above was read as forbidding the citation that requirement produces. **A commit that cannot affect a check leaves that check's evidence standing.** *Could have invalidated it* is a condition, and a commit that fails it does not reach the claim — so a run taken before a later commit is still evidence for the tree after it, provided the report names that commit and says why it is inert for that check. What decides it is what the check reads, never what kind of change the commit is. A comment-only or documentation-only commit to content a check does not read is inert for that check; the same comment is not inert for a check that reads comments, which a judged lint does, so that one is re-run or named as not re-checked. A commit touching anything a check reads is not inert for it, however small. Two dispatches of one node, about 45 minutes each, were refused over nothing but a comment-only final commit after their cited check runs, with no change in whether either tree was correct, and the manager had to send *re-run after every commit* three separate times to get past it: read as absolute, the conditional rule above is one no worker can meet, because every commit comes after the last run. The ordering demand this replaces — that the report come after everything else, and that anything found later be repaired and the whole report written again — is **withdrawn**. It failed six of fourteen nodes in one workstream, each with complete committed work, a green deterministic tier, and no acceptance criterion found unmet, and two of those carried an escalated warning about it in their own task and failed anyway. A bar finished work cannot clear teaches everyone to route around the thing that enforces quality; the property above is what that demand was serving, and it is what survives. ### State the bar in `## Acceptance criteria`, not only here A judge reads this node's `## Acceptance criteria` and its own review bar. Where the criteria are silent about something the bar demands, it imports the demand and applies its own reading of it — and finished, gate-green work has been failed twice that way: once for running the gate's parts separately, and once for never having *"provided a final verified completion report"*, a demand in neither the task nor the shared completion clause. So every demand this node will be held to is stated as a criterion of its own, including the two the bar makes of every implementation dispatch: - the behavior this node adds is **proven end to end** by a test or journey that drives the real interface, rather than by inspection; - every claim the dispatch makes about the finished work — what it verified, and the evidence for it — is **true of the tree as it finally stands**. Criteria state properties of the finished tree; the commands that produce them belong in this section. Whether the criteria answer every demand their own bar — or this appendix — makes of them is read by `just review-plan `, which spends a judged turn on it and judges it by meaning: criteria that state a demand in their own words answer it, and no criterion is refused for failing to use a particular phrase. Nothing reads it deterministically any more, because the phrase matching that did refused wordings the same review had just asked for.

## What

Make a harness run's history say what it was asked and where it is from the moment the run begins, so that every consumer can point at a conversation while it is still happening. Start from `dag-ui-project-centric-spike-transcript-source-report` (its "Q2 — live", "Q4 — addressable" and design findings), which measured both gaps on this host: the prompt reaches the history file only on the closing `type: run` line, 28-31 s after the turn began and never for a run that was killed, and an embedder learns a run's history location only from the returned report.

**The contract.** Its one authoritative statement is the Rust types in `crates/oneharness-core/src/domain/history.rs` and the stream-line types beside them, from which this repository already generates its JSON schema and its SDK types (`npm/oneharness-sdk/src/generated/`); the docs, `onejudge` and `oneagentgraph` restate it from there, and the repository's existing generated-types drift check is what goes red if a copy parts from it.
1. **Opening history line.** `HistoryWriter::begin_harness_run` (`crates/oneharness-core/src/io/history.rs`) appends, before the harness process is spawned, one line `{"type": "run-started", "schema_version": <the moved history schema version>, "history_id": string (the candidate run's UUIDv7, the same id its closing `type: run` line and its `type: event` lines carry), "harness_id": string, "prompt": string (the whole prompt, never cut), "started": RFC 3339 UTC string}` and flushes it. The history schema version moves one minor step (1.10 to 1.11) by this repository's convention. The closing `type: run` line, every `type: event` line and their fields are unchanged; a reader of the earlier schema reads the new file except the new line.
2. **In-process location.** `EventSink` gains a provided method `fn run_began(&mut self, begun: &RunBegun) -> SinkStep` whose default returns `SinkStep::Continue`, called once per harness candidate before that candidate's first `event` call, where `RunBegun` is a public struct of `harness_id`, `history_id`, `history_dir` (absolute store path), `history_project` (project slug) and `history_session` (file stem), the names `oneharness-session` and the pointer file already spell. Not called when history is off. An existing sink implementing only `event` compiles and behaves as before.
3. **Stream location.** `oneharness run --stream` writes, before a candidate's first event line, one NDJSON line `{"type": "run-started", "harness_id", "history_id", "history_dir", "history_project", "history_session"}` carrying the same values, when history is on.
4. **Retention, stated.** The history docs state the store's retention rule: a session file is removed only by an explicit `oneharness history clear --yes`; nothing else in oneharness prunes, rotates or moves the store. Today's behaviour already matches; this makes it the stated contract other repositories rely on when they journal references into it.

**Title.** Each piece is an addition. If this repository's semver check reports a public item changed incompatibly (an exhaustive public enum gaining the new stream-line variant, for example), announce the break with `!` in the form its release policy requires and say in the change which public item broke.

## Why

Every reader of a running agent's conversation (the run views a manager supervises from, the observer, and the browser view) can show the whole prompt and every tool call only if the one complete transcript says what the run was asked and where it lives while the run is still going. Today a dispatch in flight, or one whose harness was killed, has no prompt on disk at all, so readers fall back to copies cut to a few kilobytes; recording both at the run's start removes the reason those copies exist.

## Acceptance criteria

- A test driving the real `oneharness run` CLI with history on, the paid harness behind it doubled at its existing `ONEHARNESS_BIN_<ID>` seam and held before it emits anything, reads the history file while the harness is still held and finds the `run-started` line carrying the whole prompt (longer than 4,096 bytes in the test) and the `history_id` that the run's later `type: event` and closing `type: run` lines carry.
- With a two-candidate fallback chain whose first candidate fails, the same file holds two `run-started` lines with distinct `history_id`s, and `--stream` writes each candidate's `run-started` stream line, with the values its history line carries, before that candidate's first event line, both proven by tests over the real CLI.
- A test over the library's streaming run shows an `EventSink` that implements `run_began` receives, once per candidate and before that candidate's first event, a `RunBegun` whose fields locate the file the run writes, and a sink implementing only `event` receives the same events as before.
- The generated JSON schema and SDK types carry the `run-started` history and stream lines, regenerated from the Rust types, and the history docs state both lines, `run_began`, the moved schema version and the store's retention rule.
- The tests over the code this change touches are green on the finished tree: `oneharness-core`'s history and streaming tests, the CLI's run tests and the generated-types drift check.
- The judged llmlint tier of `oneharness` over this change's diff against its base reports no failing rule.
- Tests through both real oneharness run --stream and the library streaming run with history disabled prove no run-started notification line and no EventSink::run_began call, while existing event behavior is preserved.
- Every claim the dispatch makes about the finished implementation, verification and evidence remains accurate for the final tree. Evidence from an earlier tree is explicitly identified as such, with subsequent changes and corrections stated; no superseded result is presented as verification of the finished tree.

## Spike evidence

This task builds on these spikes. Start from each report's measurements and from the
harness on each branch rather than measuring again. A report is the document of this plan's
own project with that id or, on a copy of the plan, the one whose `onetaskgraph.origin`
names it:

## Additional info

### Operational notes for this host

**Run only the checks that exercise what you changed.** The tests that cover the code
you touched, the lint that reads your diff — and nothing wider. The repository's own
automation runs the full bar downstream on the change this work becomes: a `pre-push`
hook where that repository publishes locally, the host's required checks where it
publishes remotely. Neither is waiting for you to have run it first, so running it here
spends twenty to forty minutes of this dispatch learning what the merge path reports
anyway. That is measured rather than estimated: one node in this workstream spent about
84 minutes on three rounds of everything its repository could run, to reach lint findings
a diff-scoped run reports in two.

**Pick those checks from your change, and take the narrowest scope each one supports.**
One test module over the whole suite; the lint over your diff over the lint over the
tree. A repository's own fast deterministic tier is a fine choice when it is what
exercises your change — its `just --list` says which recipe that is — and a poor one when
you reached for it because it was the widest thing available. When a check you ran
reports something, fix that and run **that check** again; nothing here asks you to re-run
its neighbours to confirm, and a wider tier cannot re-check a finding it never made.

**A dispatch that changed nothing tracked owes none of them.** When your deliverable is a
document, a report, or an answer, there is no changed code for those checks to exercise
and you are complete without them — decide that from what the repository shows, never
because running them is slow or inconvenient. `git status` reporting nothing to commit is
then a correct and complete outcome, not a problem to solve by writing a file nobody
asked for.

**A publication check runs downstream, so no worker can run it and none is judged on it.**
The host's required checks and a repository's `pre-push` gate run on the change this
work becomes, after this dispatch settles: downstream publication checks are not
runnable by a worker, and a dispatch is never held to one having passed. That holds on a
retry too. A `checks-failed` retry — a re-dispatch onto the same branch carrying the
merge path's refusal and `onevcs`'s evidence — is judged on its task's stated local
acceptance checks: the repair of what the refusal named, proven by the checks the task
names, and never by the downstream check passing again, which can only happen once the
retry has settled. One retry that fixed and locally verified the failing test its
refusal named was failed for not re-running the required check, which left finished
work unpublished and its dependents skipped until a manager published it by hand.

**Never signal a process you did not identify by PID, and a PID you got from a pattern is
still a pattern kill.** Several managers share this host, and their dispatches, drivers,
publications and test servers run under the same few binary names — `just`, `node`,
`python`, `onepipeline-api` — so a kill by name knows nothing about *whose* work it
matched. The distinction is the tool rather than the pattern: `pgrep` and `ps` **read**,
and either spelling of them is fine, `pgrep -x` included; `pkill` **signals**, and it is
never the answer here, in any spelling. `-x` is the trap, because it reads as the careful
one — `pkill -f 'just gate'` at least needs a narrowing pattern, while `pkill -x just`
takes every `just` on the machine. Reading the table first and piping the pids into `kill`
is no way around it: that is the same pattern kill with more steps.

Two workers reached that place from different directions on 2026-08-24, while another
manager's dispatch had been live over an hour. One ran `pkill -TERM -x just`. The other
ran `ps -eo pid,args | grep 'onepipeline-api serve' | awk '{print $1}' | while read pid;
do kill "$pid"; done` — which obeys the letter of every paragraph below and does the same
damage, because `just dag-ui` and the e2e suites both spawn that server and a pytest run's
were alive at that moment.

**The one process you may signal is one you started yourself, so capture its PID as you
start it:**

    cmd & MYPID=$!
    kill "$MYPID"

Anything you did not start belongs to somebody. Read what it is, report what you found,
and leave it running.

**A wait written against a full command line never ends, because one of those command
lines is yours.** That is a different defect from the one above — it wedges your own
dispatch rather than somebody else's — and it is why `pgrep -f` cannot be waited on.
`pgrep -f` matches its pattern against every process's whole argv and excludes exactly one
process — itself — never the shell that invoked it. So any pattern naming the thing you are
waiting for is, by construction, a substring of the command line of the shell doing the
waiting: `until ! pgrep -f "just gate"` matches its own loop and never exits, and so does
the same loop written against the judged lint tier's script, `scripts/fetch-corpus.sh`,
or `publish-branch`. That is a defect in the polling mechanism rather than a fact about gates,
so it applies to every wait you write.

That has wedged four workers here, and then two more workers and the manager itself in one
night: seven instances of one defect. A crozier corpus audit waited in `until ! pgrep -f
'scripts/fetch-corpus.sh'` with no fetch running at all — the only two matches were its own
polling shell and the manager's diagnostic shell — and waited until it was interrupted. A
`check-plan-bar-conflict` dispatch waited on `! pgrep -f` naming the judged lint tier's
script, whose negation could never become true, and was cancelled and killed; its replacement then reached for
`pkill -f` against three patterns, which is not a wait at all but the same self-match with a
signal attached, and is refused above. And the manager, an hour after instructing a worker
about this, guarded a launch with `pgrep -f "publish-branch" && echo ABORT || launch`, whose
pattern was a literal substring of the launching shell's own command line: it aborted
unconditionally and then reported a publish as RUNNING that did not exist. That last one is
the evidence that matters most — a rule its own author reproduces an hour after issuing it
is a rule whose wording is the problem rather than its reader.

**Wait with a sentinel file.** Background the whole command you are waiting on — one
command, so that what you waited on is what you meant to run — and poll for a file only
that invocation can write:

    ( just test > /tmp/check.$$.log 2>&1; echo $? > /tmp/check.$$.exit ) &
    until [ -f /tmp/check.$$.exit ]; do sleep 20; done

**A process must finish inside the turn that started it.** Backgrounding is how you wait
on a slow command *within* one turn, which is why the launch and the wait sit together in
that example — both halves belong to the same turn. What does not survive is a background
process left running when the turn ends: nothing carries it across, and the launch gives
you no sign of that, because it succeeded and the turn then ended normally. The loss
shows up a turn later as a sentinel that never appeared and a recipe terminated by
signal, with the whole run to pay for again. It bites hardest where it is most tempting,
because a worker reaches for backgrounding exactly when a command is slow enough to
threaten the turn — here the judged lint tier and a whole test tier, which are the two
runs a node most needs to have made. So run a slow check in the foreground, or background
it and wait out its sentinel before your turn ends; never end a turn intending to read a
result on the next one.

**To ask whether a process is running at all, match the executable, not the command line.**
`pgrep -x onepipeline` matches process *names* exactly — the binary, not its arguments — so
the shell doing the asking, whose own name is `bash`, cannot match it however the pattern
is spelled. Where the binary name is not distinctive enough to identify what you mean
(`just`, `node` and `python` run everything), read the process table instead and drop the
one self-match that form has:

    ps -eo pid,args | grep -v grep | grep 'lint-llm-diff'

Both of those are **reads**, which is what makes `-x` safe here and forbidden the moment
the tool signals. The replacement for the worker wedged above reached for `pkill -f "just
gate"`, `pkill -f "just check"` and `pkill -f "nx run"` while another manager's run was
live. Read to learn what is running, report what you found, and signal nothing you did not
start.

**One sentinel and one log per invocation, and look before you launch one.** That pair is a
shape rather than two literal paths. Several dispatches run on this host at once and they
share `/tmp`, so a second worker writing `/tmp/check.log` writes into the first one's — and
`until [ -f /tmp/check.exit ]` returns immediately on somebody else's exit file, reporting
their result as yours. Name both after the invocation (`/tmp/check.$$.log`, or the node
id), and, before starting it, check whether its sentinel path is already in use by another
invocation; if so, choose a different invocation-specific pair. This path-ownership check
does not prohibit concurrent checks or judged tiers. Three workers collided on shared names
today and not one of the three failures read as what it was: two
deterministic-tier runs deadlocked against the same cargo target-directory lock, so both
logs sat unchanged and neither progressed — about fifteen minutes lost and three
interruptions to a live turn; two whole-e2e runs wrote to one log, and stopping the
duplicate left four `SIGTERM` entries in it that read exactly like real test failures; two
judged-tier runs raced and wasted a roll, which was harmless only by luck. Read a log that
has stopped growing as two commands blocking each other before you read it as one command
working.

**Root-owned files after a container run.** The pre-push visual guard captures in Docker
as root and can leave `.nx/` and `dist/` unwritable, failing the *next* check with `NX
Permission denied (os error 13)`. There is no passwordless sudo; repair from inside a

**If a test fails in a way that makes no sense, check the host before the test.** On
2026-08-19 two publication attempts against the same already-green branch failed on two

**If a rule looks wrong or misapplied, say so with evidence rather than editing it.**

**One suppression policy, and this is the whole of it.** A site-scoped `ignore` directive
is permitted where the rule is genuinely misapplied at that site **and** the directive
carries a substantive reason saying why. What is forbidden is silencing a finding you
have not answered so that a count moves. What you owe an account of is **every
suppression your own diff writes — added, moved or rewritten — and every one already

Suppressions elsewhere in the tree are not yours to inventory: this repository carries several hundred standing directives, and
a list of them would be longer than the report is read under while saying nothing about

That scope is stated because the sentence it replaces read two ways at once: its first

node was failed on the wider reading for not accounting for suppressions it had never

and the scale both support, and it is written so that a worker complying with it and a

refuse, and if the two can land in different places it is not one source yet.

`AGENTS.md` states no suppression policy of its own and points here, because this file is
what your judge reads beside your task: while that document said it twice, one
dispatch added four site-scoped ignores each carrying a substantive reason and was failed
for *"the task's categorical instruction never to suppress a rule"* — work that was
correct under one of this repository's own readings and refused under the other.

**`--no-verify` is not an acceptable response to a slow or inconvenient hook.** The hooks
are this repository's enforcement point — there is no CI — so bypassing one commits work
that nothing has checked, and nothing you run afterwards catches it: a check runs over
the finished tree, by which point a bypassed commit is simply history. Two workers
today reached for `git commit --no-verify`, both on a commit they had judged mechanical,
and one of the two was a *merge* commit — a conflict resolution, which is the single most
likely commit in a dispatch to be wrong. No check caught either one; the monitor caught

**Commit a coherent working piece the moment it works.** A dirty worktree does not
survive this dispatch: what is uncommitted when your last turn ends is what nothing
recovers — not a retry, not a recovery verb, not a manager reading the branch. So each
piece is its own commit as you finish it, rather than one commit held back to the end.

are run before it is committed rather than after, so that each commit is one you have
evidence for.

**Ask rather than stop.** When you cannot proceed without a decision that is not yours —

would have to relax — put the question to your manager over `$ORCHESTRATOR_ASK_MANAGER`,

nothing can recover: a worker that reasoned about a frozen contract correctly, declined to
amend it unilaterally, named two options for its owner, and then stopped for three turns
lost about fifteen minutes of correct work and settled reporting `ahead of main: 0
commit(s)`.

**Draft a follow-up that can wait; never draft one that cannot.** Work you notice that
is outside your subtask — a bug beside the code you touched, a missing test or script, a
stale document, an improvement to this harness or to the context agents are given — is a
follow-up, and doing it is not yours. Record each one the moment you notice it by piping
its body into `"$ORCHESTRATOR_FOLLOW_UP_DRAFT"`, whose `--help` names the flags and the four

a list at the end of your last message instead, because nothing reads that list. A draft is
unverified — a follow-up agent checks every one after the run — and it is not your
completion report, which still says what you did. Drafting is only for what can wait:
anything blocking, whether a decision fork, a constraint you cannot meet, or something your
manager should act on now, goes over `$ORCHESTRATOR_ASK_MANAGER` immediately, as the
paragraph above says, and is never drafted in its place.

**A GitHub rate-limit refusal that `gh api rate_limit` disagrees with is the secondary
limiter.** The primary limit is the one that endpoint reports and the one a wait answers.
The secondary limiter is reported by nothing, polled by nothing, and not waited out by
polling — every further attempt extends it. So when a `gh` call is refused for a rate
limit while `gh api rate_limit` still shows budget, stop making that call: deliver the
result another way, name in your report what was refused and what you tried, and leave the
retry to a person.

**Publication goes through the harness.** The session branch reaches its remote only
through `onevcs publish "$ONEVCS_SESSION"`, and its change request is lifted, landed or
kept for the user's review by the lifecycle after you settle. No `git push` of the session branch, no `gh pr create`
for it, no `gh pr ready`, no `gh pr merge`. Finish the branch, commit everything, leave
the tree clean, and report. Landing it is explicitly **not** yours to perform and **not**
part of your acceptance criteria. Two things are yours, and each only when this task's
own `## Additional info` — its own words above these notes — says so:

- **Only when the task's `## Additional info` says the change request may be published
  early**: `onevcs publish "$ONEVCS_SESSION" --draft [--title T] [--body-file PATH]` opens
  the session's change request as a draft, and a later `publish --draft` pushes new
  commits onto that same change request and never opens a second. Commit everything
  first — a dirty tree is committed for you, under a provenance you did not choose.
  `onevcs change describe "$ONEVCS_SESSION" --body-file PATH` replaces its description
  and `onevcs change show "$ONEVCS_SESSION"` reads it back. The description you leave is
  what the drafter finishes from, so start it with what only you know — the evidence and
  where it is. Never mark the draft ready yourself; after you finish, the lifecycle lifts
  it or keeps it as a draft for the user's review according to the repository's policy.
  `ONEVCS_SESSION` is in every lifecycle dispatch's environment.
- **Only when the task's `## Additional info` authorizes a throwaway demonstration change
  request**: after the draft is open, cut a branch from the session branch, commit the
  demonstration on it, push it with `git push -u origin <branch>`, open it with
  `gh pr create --draft --base <session branch> --head <branch> --title "DO NOT MERGE: …"`,

  anything — then close it with `gh pr close <n> --delete-branch`, return to the session
  branch, and delete the local branch — a local branch left behind makes the session's
  close refuse. Its base is always the session branch, never the repository's base; it
  is never marked ready; it is closed before you finish.

Everything else a push or a change-request verb could do is still not yours.

**A branch you resume may already be on its remote, and a published branch only grows.**
A retry — a `checks-failed` one among them — re-dispatches onto the same branch, which an
earlier publication may already have pushed. So check before you touch its history: `git
fetch` and `git log origin/<branch>`, or the published commit your task's context names.
The repair of a branch already on its remote is new commits on top of the remote's
commit — never an amend, a rebase, a squash, a reset or a force-push of commits already
there. One retry that fixed both refusals its merge path named by amending the two commits
already pushed was refused `non-fast-forward` when it published, and settled
`push-rejected` with the correct tree stranded on the host.

**Every claim you make about the finished work is true of the tree as it finally
stands.** That is the property you are held to, and it says nothing about where your
report sits. This conversation does not end when you report — your supervisor keeps
asking, and answering well means running things — so a report required to be this
dispatch's literal final output is one no correct worker can give. What is required
instead is that nothing you have said about the work is untrue of the tree by the time you
stop.

When work follows your report, say in that same turn what changed and what you re-ran. A
correct delta satisfies this exactly as fully as restating the whole report does. Silence
does not satisfy it at all. Your last substantive turn should leave a reader able to say
what the finished tree contains and what was verified about it, whether that comes from
one report or from a report plus the deltas after it.

**A claim about a check, a test, a lint run, or a commit that was not run or was not made
is false, and fails on its merits.** A report asserting a check passed on a commit where
no such run occurred is that case, and one node of this host's history was correctly
failed for it. So do not carry a claim forward across a change that could have invalidated
it — re-run what the change could have broken, or say which claims you have not re-checked.

**Evidence deliberately about an earlier or induced state is not a false claim.** Proving
that an assertion can fail means making it fail, reading the message, and reverting;
proving that a message used to say nothing means quoting the run from before the change.
A citation of a run taken before a change, or of a failure induced on purpose as evidence,
is correct evidence — provided the citation says which it is. One node of this host was
failed for exactly that: its own criteria required its assertions be observed failing, and
the resulting-tree property above was read as forbidding the citation that requirement
produces.

**A commit that cannot affect a check leaves that check's evidence standing.** *Could have
invalidated it* is a condition, and a commit that fails it does not reach the claim — so a
run taken before a later commit is still evidence for the tree after it, provided the
report names that commit and says why it is inert for that check. What decides it is what
the check reads, never what kind of change the commit is. A comment-only or
documentation-only commit to content a check does not read is inert for that check; the
same comment is not inert for a check that reads comments, which a judged lint does, so
that one is re-run or named as not re-checked. A commit touching anything a check reads is
not inert for it, however small. Two dispatches of one node, about 45 minutes each, were
refused over nothing but a comment-only final commit after their cited check runs, with no
change in whether either tree was correct, and the manager had to send *re-run after every
commit* three separate times to get past it: read as absolute, the conditional rule above
is one no worker can meet, because every commit comes after the last run.

The ordering demand this replaces — that the report come after everything else, and that
anything found later be repaired and the whole report written again — is **withdrawn**. It
failed six of fourteen nodes in one workstream, each with complete committed work, a green
deterministic tier, and no acceptance criterion found unmet, and two of those carried an
escalated warning about it in their own task and failed anyway. A bar finished work
cannot clear teaches everyone to route around the thing that enforces quality; the
property above is what that demand was serving, and it is what survives.

### State the bar in `## Acceptance criteria`, not only here

A judge reads this node's `## Acceptance criteria` and its own review bar. Where the
criteria are silent about something the bar demands, it imports the demand and applies its
own reading of it — and finished, gate-green work has been failed twice that way: once for
running the gate's parts separately, and once for never having *"provided a final verified
completion report"*, a demand in neither the task nor the shared completion clause.

So every demand this node will be held to is stated as a criterion of its own, including
the two the bar makes of every implementation dispatch:

- the behavior this node adds is **proven end to end** by a test or journey that drives the
  real interface, rather than by inspection;
- every claim the dispatch makes about the finished work — what it verified, and the
  evidence for it — is **true of the tree as it finally stands**.

Criteria state properties of the finished tree; the commands that produce them belong in
this section. Whether the criteria answer every demand their own bar — or this appendix —
